_doc: Published by pipeline/standards_publish.mjs from pipeline/standards.json. Never edited by hand.

account_executive.label: Account Executive or SDR
account_executive.summary: Sales loops are live role-plays and small written or recorded pieces: a mock cold call or discovery call, often run twice to see how you take feedback, a cold email, a voicemail, a mock demo. Several employers publish theirs.

shows.label: A cold call
shows.means: Open, state the problem you solve, handle the first objection, ask for the meeting.
artifacts: A call script: opener, problem statement, objection responses
A recording of yourself running it
A 30-second voicemail pitch

shows.label: A discovery call
shows.means: Plan the questions that surface the buyer's problem and what it costs them. Ask them in order.
artifacts: A discovery call plan for one real company

shows.label: Taking feedback
shows.means: Run the call, critique it yourself, take one note and run it again better.
artifacts: Two recordings of the same call with what you changed

shows.label: An outbound sequence
shows.means: Pick a real prospect. Research them, write the cold email, and say why this account, this person and these words.
artifacts: A cold email to a researched prospect with a short rationale
A target account list with a sequence of short emails
The reply and meeting numbers, if you send them

shows.label: A qualified deal
shows.means: Take one real or realistic opportunity and say who decides, on what, by when and why.
artifacts: A deal sheet filled in for one opportunity

shows.label: A pitch that teaches the buyer something
shows.means: Reframe one buyer's problem with a fact they did not know. Tailor it to one person.
artifacts: A short insight pitch for a named role at a real company

shows.label: A product demo
shows.means: Demo a real product to a pretend buyer. Fit it to their problem, then send the follow-up email with next steps.
artifacts: A short recorded demo of a product you know
A follow-up proposal email

shows.label: A plan for your first months
shows.means: Say which accounts you would go after first, how you would build pipeline, and what you expect by when.
artifacts: A short pipeline and ramp plan for one real company's product

bizops.label: Business Operations Manager
bizops.summary: BizOps and Strategy & Operations loops centre on a take-home: a dataset, a day or two, then slides or a memo defended live. Startups add a paid work trial. Big tech companies do not publish their loops; the detail comes from two startups' own pages, DoorDash's careers blog and practitioners.

shows.label: A structured answer to a business problem
shows.means: Break a company's problem into parts. Size each and commit to a recommendation.
artifacts: A written answer to a case about a real company

shows.label: An analysis that ends in a recommendation
shows.means: Take a real dataset and a business question. Do the analysis, rank what to do with the expected return, state your assumptions, and defend it live.
artifacts: A deck or memo from a dataset: ranked recommendations, expected return, assumptions, a plan with milestones
A recorded walk-through answering hard questions on it

shows.label: Answer-first writing
shows.means: Lead with the answer. Put each supporting point under it.
artifacts: A one-page memo or short deck with one governing point

shows.label: A metric and a rhythm to run it by
shows.means: Pick the few numbers a team should watch and the meeting where they are read.
artifacts: A small dashboard and a one-page operating review for a real or student organisation

shows.label: A working tool built with AI
shows.means: Build a small internal tool on real or synthetic data, such as a customer-health view, and use it to do one piece of work.
artifacts: A demo of a self-built app or workflow
The work it produced, such as outreach drafted from the view

shows.label: An impact story with numbers
shows.means: Write up one piece of work: the problem, what you did, the number that moved.
artifacts: One project write-up with a measured result

brand_manager.label: Brand Manager
brand_manager.summary: Brand hiring asks for a short brand case answered from the consumer, and stories of leading people. No employer publishes its marketing case; the case detail comes from student accounts on one school's site, and the planning steps from a course and a book.

shows.label: A brand case answered from the consumer
shows.means: Take a short brand problem. Start from the consumer, look at the company and its competitors, then work through product, price, place and promotion. State your assumptions and commit to one recommendation tied to a consumer insight.
artifacts: A one-page written answer to a brand problem for a real product
A recorded spoken answer to the same case

shows.label: A brand plan for one product
shows.means: Pick a real brand. Research its buyers, segment them, choose a target and write the positioning. Set objectives, then plan product, packaging, communication, price and retail execution.
artifacts: A brand plan: research, segments, target, positioning, objectives and the mix
A one-page summary of the plan's main decisions

shows.label: A growth argument from buying evidence
shows.means: Say how a brand will grow. Argue from reaching more buyers, and from making the brand easier to think of and easier to buy. Say what the evidence is.
artifacts: A short memo on where one brand's next buyers come from

shows.label: Stories of leading and getting results
shows.means: Write up times you led people, made a timely decision and got a result through others. Keep each story to the situation, what you did and what changed.
artifacts: Three written behavioral stories from real projects, clubs or jobs

business_analytics.label: Business Analytics Manager
business_analytics.summary: Analytics loops test SQL and a product-metrics case: define the metrics, plan the experiment, read the result. Meta publishes its first screen and P&G describes its analytics function; no source read names a dashboard or report as the work sample.

shows.label: SQL on a business question
shows.means: Take a question about a product or a business. Write the SQL that answers it and explain the result.
artifacts: A set of solved SQL problems, each tied to a business question

shows.label: A product-metrics case
shows.means: Pick a product. Define what success means in metrics. Say how you would test a change and what result would make you ship it.
artifacts: A written metrics case for one product: success metrics, the experiment, how to read the result

shows.label: An experiment design and readout
shows.means: Design an experiment: the hypothesis, the metric, the unit, the sample size and the guardrails. Analyse a real or public result and write the decision.
artifacts: An experiment design document
An experiment readout with a recommendation

shows.label: An analysis of what drives a business
shows.means: Combine sales or purchase data with what consumers say. Find what drives the result, measure the effect of one promotion or campaign, and recommend a change to pricing, media or product.
artifacts: An analysis that joins a public sales dataset with consumer research
A recommendation with the measured effect behind it

business_intelligence.label: Business Intelligence Manager
business_intelligence.summary: No employer publishes a BI loop. Job-posting snippets and two paid prep sites point to SQL and a take-home analysis that ends in a recommendation. No source read names a dashboard as the work sample.

shows.label: SQL for analytics questions
shows.means: Frame a product or business question. Pull the data with SQL and use basic statistics to reach an answer.
artifacts: A set of solved SQL and analytics problems with your reasoning

shows.label: A take-home analysis
shows.means: Take a dataset and a question. Do the analysis in SQL or Python and write up the answer as a business recommendation.
artifacts: A written-up analysis of one dataset that ends in a recommendation
The queries or notebook behind it

chief_of_staff.label: Chief of Staff
chief_of_staff.summary: Chief of staff hiring leans on a work sample: a real assignment that mimics the job, presented and defended. The sources are a practitioner article and two startups' pages; most other writing defines the role and says nothing about hiring.

shows.label: A trial project for a principal
shows.means: Take a real problem a company's leader faces. Write the plan or the analysis, then present it and take questions.
artifacts: A written plan or analysis on one real company problem
Priority or board materials drafted for a leader, real or from a student organization
A recorded presentation of it

shows.label: Answer-first writing
shows.means: Lead with the answer. Put each supporting point under it.
artifacts: A one-page memo with one governing point

shows.label: Stories about hard calls
shows.means: Write up a hard decision you made, a time you moved people who did not want to move, and how you weighed a proposal.
artifacts: Three short write-ups, each with the decision and your reasoning

comp_benefits.label: Compensation and Benefits Manager
comp_benefits.summary: No employer source says what a compensation candidate must show. The compensation credential's outline does say what the work is: price jobs against the market, build a base pay structure, design variable pay.

shows.label: Jobs priced against the market
shows.means: Take a handful of jobs and public pay data. Match each job, bring the data to one date, blend the sources and set a market rate for each.
artifacts: A spreadsheet pricing five to ten jobs, with the sources and each adjustment shown

shows.label: A base pay structure
shows.means: Build grades and pay ranges for a small company from your market rates. Place each job in a grade and say which rules you checked.
artifacts: A pay structure: grades, ranges and where each job sits
A one-page note on the approach and the rules checked

shows.label: A variable pay plan with its cost
shows.means: Design a bonus or incentive plan for one team. Say what it pays for, model what it costs under a few outcomes, and write the note that explains it to employees.
artifacts: A plan design with a cost model
A one-page employee note

compliance.label: Compliance Manager
compliance.summary: No employer program or loop was found for compliance. Four credential outlines name the work: program design, due diligence and investigations, and testing controls. Two of the four were read only from search results.

shows.label: A compliance risk assessment and program
shows.means: Pick a small company in a regulated field. Assess where it could break the rules, then outline the program: policies, training, monitoring and how concerns get investigated.
artifacts: A compliance risk assessment
A one-page program outline with the training plan

shows.label: A due diligence and investigation write-up
shows.means: Take a public financial crime case or a synthetic set of transactions. Do the customer due diligence, find the transactions that look wrong and write up the case.
artifacts: A case write-up: the customer, the red flags, the transactions and the decision

shows.label: A test of one control
shows.means: Pick one rule a process must follow. Plan how to test it, test a sample and report what failed and what to fix.
artifacts: A test plan and a findings memo for one control

corp_dev.label: Corporate Development Manager
corp_dev.summary: No corporate development loop is published. A valuation textbook covers the models and a venture firm's published memos show the written recommendation; neither is a hiring source.

shows.label: A valuation of a real company
shows.means: Value one public company three ways: comparable companies, precedent transactions and discounted cash flow. Say why the answers differ.
artifacts: A comparable companies table and a precedents table
A discounted cash flow model
A one-page summary of the value range

shows.label: A merger analysis
shows.means: Pick a real or plausible deal. Model what the buyer pays, how it is financed and what it does to the buyer's earnings.
artifacts: A merger model for one deal with a short read-out

shows.label: A recommendation memo for a deal
shows.means: Pick a target for a real acquirer. Write the recommendation: the business, the market, the diligence you did, the risks and the terms you would propose.
artifacts: A written memo recommending one acquisition or investment

corp_strategy_analyst.label: Corporate Strategy Analyst or Associate
corp_strategy_analyst.summary: No employer publishes a loop for this role. A job posting names the work, a vendor guide describes the case and a book covers the writing.

shows.label: A structured answer to a company's own problem
shows.means: Take a real question a company faces, such as build, buy or partner. Lay out the options, put them in order and commit to one.
artifacts: A written answer to a case about a real company

shows.label: An analysis that ends in a recommendation
shows.means: Define the problem. Run the analysis on real data, build the model and recommend what to do, as you would to an executive.
artifacts: A deck or memo from a dataset with a model behind it
A recorded walk-through of the recommendation

shows.label: Answer-first writing
shows.means: Lead with the answer. Put each supporting point under it.
artifacts: A one-page memo or short deck with one governing point

corporate_banking.label: Corporate Banking Associate
corporate_banking.summary: No bank publishes a loop for this role. One credential's outline lists seven areas of credit work, which together read as a credit memo; job postings seen only in search ask for formal credit training. Both items are thin.

shows.label: A financial and cash flow assessment of a borrower
shows.means: Pick a company with public filings. Read its statements, work out its cash flow and say whether it can repay.
artifacts: A financial statement and cash flow analysis of one company

shows.label: A credit memo
shows.means: Write up one borrower: its industry and competitors, its management, its finances, the collateral, where repayment comes from and how you would structure the loan. Name the signs that would tell you the loan is going wrong.
artifacts: A credit memo on one real company with a proposed loan structure

customer_success.label: Customer Success Leader
customer_success.summary: No source read describes a customer success loop: Salesforce's hiring page is general and names no step for this role. One book defines the work, so both items rest on it alone.

shows.label: A customer health score
shows.means: Pick a product. Say which signals show a customer is drifting, how you would score them and which retention numbers you would watch.
artifacts: A customer health score definition with the metrics behind it

shows.label: An onboarding playbook for one segment
shows.means: Choose one customer segment of a real product. Write how you get them to the promised result fast, who does what across teams, and how much contact that segment gets.
artifacts: A success plan or onboarding playbook for one segment

data_engineer.label: Data Engineer
data_engineer.summary: Data engineer loops test SQL, Python and data modeling on a product scenario; a public course and two books describe the pipeline work behind them. Meta confirms only its format; the round content is from prep vendors.

shows.label: SQL and Python on data
shows.means: Write the SQL queries and the Python that transform raw data into the tables a question needs. Write them without help and explain each step.
artifacts: A set of solved SQL problems with your reasoning
A Python data-transformation script with tests

shows.label: A data model for a product
shows.means: Pick a product. Define the metrics someone would ask for. Design the tables that serve them and say why you shaped them that way.
artifacts: Metric definitions for one product scenario
A dimensional data model sketched for it

shows.label: An end-to-end pipeline
shows.means: Take a real dataset. Ingest it, orchestrate the runs, load a warehouse, transform it and serve a result. Write a README another person can reproduce it from.
artifacts: A public repository with ingestion, orchestration, a warehouse, transformations with tests and a dashboard
A README that lets someone else run it

shows.label: A design write-up with the trade-offs
shows.means: For one data system, say how it stores and processes data. Explain what you chose for reliability, scale and upkeep, and what each choice costs.
artifacts: A short design document for a data system: storage, batch or stream processing, and the trade-offs

data_scientist.label: Data Scientist
data_scientist.summary: Product data loops test SQL written live, a product-metrics case and experiment design. Take-homes are an analysis of a dataset with a written answer.

shows.label: SQL on real data
shows.means: Answer product questions with queries you write yourself.
artifacts: A set of queries on a public dataset, each with the question it answers

shows.label: A product-metrics case
shows.means: Define success for a product. Pick the metrics, say how each could mislead, and add guardrails.
artifacts: A metric framework for a product you use

shows.label: An experiment, designed and read
shows.means: Write the hypothesis, the unit, the metric, the sample size and the guardrails. Read a result and decide.
artifacts: An experiment design and a readout

shows.label: An analysis of a dataset, written up
shows.means: Take a dataset and a question. Do the analysis and write an answer a manager could act on.
artifacts: A notebook or report with the question, the method, the answer and its limits

shows.label: A metric drop, diagnosed
shows.means: Given a metric that fell, list the causes, check each against data, and say which it is.
artifacts: A short diagnosis write-up with the checks you ran

digital_transformation.label: Digital Transformation Manager
digital_transformation.summary: No employer source describes this loop. Two credentials describe the work: a change plan for a live project and a record of projects led. Both items are thin.

shows.label: A change plan for a real project
shows.means: Pick a change under way in an organization you know, such as a new system. Assess the risk and how ready people are, then plan sponsors, stakeholders and communication.
artifacts: A risk and readiness assessment for one change
A change management strategy with its core plans

shows.label: A record of projects you led
shows.means: For each project, say what you were responsible for: the plan, the decisions, the delivery and the outcome.
artifacts: A write-up per project with your responsibility and the result

enterprise_risk.label: Enterprise Risk Manager
enterprise_risk.summary: No employer program or loop was found for enterprise risk. Three credential outlines say what the work is: assess an organization's risks from its business model, measure financial risk, and review controls.

shows.label: A risk assessment of one organization
shows.means: Pick a real company. Analyze how it makes money, list the risks to that, rate them and say how each should be handled.
artifacts: A risk register built from the company's business model
A one-page risk strategy for its leaders

shows.label: A measure of market or credit risk
shows.means: Take a small portfolio or loan book with public data. Measure its market or credit risk with a standard model and state the model's limits.
artifacts: A workbook or notebook with the risk calculation
A short note on the result and what the model misses

shows.label: A review of one process and its controls
shows.means: Take one process, such as paying expenses in a club. Plan the review, find where it can go wrong, test the controls and report what you found.
artifacts: A short audit plan and a findings memo for one process

fpa.label: FP&A Manager
fpa.summary: No employer source describes an FP&A loop. The profession's own exam outline names the work: build a model, project revenue, explain variances, test sensitivities. A practitioner newsletter supplies the metrics and planning formats.

shows.label: A forecast model with sensitivities
shows.means: Build a model for a real company. Project revenue, state the drivers, and show how the result moves when they change.
artifacts: A spreadsheet model with a revenue projection and a sensitivity table
A one-page chart summary for a business partner

shows.label: A variance analysis
shows.means: Compare plan to actual for one period. Say which lines moved, by how much and why.
artifacts: A variance table with a short commentary
A ratio analysis from a public company's filings

fraud_risk.label: Fraud and Credit Risk Analyst
fraud_risk.summary: The only sources are two credential outlines, and they cover the investigation side: fraud schemes, investigations and prevention. No credential or published loop was found for fraud analytics roles at fintechs.

shows.label: A teardown of a real fraud scheme
shows.means: Take a public fraud case. Explain how the scheme worked, how it showed in the transactions and which control would have caught it.
artifacts: A written teardown of one fraud case with the red flags listed

shows.label: An investigation of suspect transactions
shows.means: Take a public or synthetic set of transactions. Find the ones that look wrong, gather the evidence and write the case up for a decision.
artifacts: A case file: the method, the flagged transactions, the evidence and a recommendation
The analysis file or notebook behind it

shows.label: A fraud prevention plan
shows.means: Pick a small organization. List how it could be defrauded and design the controls that prevent or deter each way.
artifacts: A fraud risk assessment with a control for each risk

growth_manager.label: Growth Manager
growth_manager.summary: No company publishes a growth manager loop. Practitioners say the same thing: show applied growth work on real products.

shows.label: How a product grows
shows.means: Draw the loop that brings a real product its users. Name the weak step.
artifacts: A drawn growth loop with each step and what feeds the next
A write-up of one company's main growth engine

shows.label: An experiment, designed and read
shows.means: Write the hypothesis, the metric, the guardrails and the sample size. Then run it and say what you decided.
artifacts: An experiment write-up: hypothesis, metrics, design, result, decision

shows.label: A growth teardown, published
shows.means: Take a real product. Show its loop, a problem in it, and the experiment you would run.
artifacts: A public teardown; several make a portfolio

shows.label: Real channel work
shows.means: Run one paid ad on a social network and one on search. Audit a real site's SEO. Report what happened.
artifacts: An ad you ran with its numbers
An SEO health check of a real site

shows.label: A funnel, measured
shows.means: Set up tracking on a real funnel. Find where people drop and propose a fix.
artifacts: A funnel analysis with the query or dashboard behind it

hr_manager.label: Human Resources Manager
hr_manager.summary: The HR leadership programs publish their rotations but not how they select. What the work is comes from two credential outlines, which weigh employee relations, engagement and pay most and test judgment in workplace situations.

shows.label: Judgment in workplace situations
shows.means: Take common workplace situations, such as a complaint against a manager or a policy applied unevenly. Write what you would do, in what order, and which policy or rule applies.
artifacts: Written answers to five HR situations, each with the steps and the reasoning

shows.label: A project in one HR area
shows.means: Pick one area the programs rotate through: employee relations, engagement, pay, hiring or learning. Do a small project in it for a club, a team or a small business, and say what should change.
artifacts: A project write-up for a real group, such as an engagement survey with findings and actions or a hiring plan

ib_associate.label: Investment Banking Associate
ib_associate.summary: The banks' program pages give eligibility and format and say nothing about interviews. The one usable source is the standard valuation textbook, so every item rests on it alone.

shows.label: A valuation of a real company
shows.means: Value one public company three ways: comparable companies, precedent transactions and discounted cash flow. Say why the answers differ.
artifacts: A comparable companies table and a precedents table
A discounted cash flow model
A one-page summary of the value range

shows.label: A leveraged buyout model
shows.means: Pick a company a buyer could take private. Model the purchase, the debt and the return at exit.
artifacts: A leveraged buyout model for one company with the returns under a few cases

shows.label: A merger analysis
shows.means: Pick a real or plausible deal. Model what the buyer pays, how it is financed and what it does to the buyer's earnings.
artifacts: A merger model for one deal with a short read-out

investment_manager.label: Investment Manager
investment_manager.summary: No investment firm's hiring page was found. The closest published form is a student competition run by the CFA Institute: an equity research report on one listed company and a short presentation to judges.

shows.label: An equity research report
shows.means: Pick one listed company. Analyze its financials, value it, and write a report that ends in a recommendation.
artifacts: A written equity research report on one public company

shows.label: A short presentation of the recommendation
shows.means: Present your recommendation in ten minutes with slides. Take questions on it.
artifacts: A recorded ten-minute presentation with slides

management_consultant.label: Management Consultant
management_consultant.summary: Consulting loops are a spoken case and a conversation about your own experience, after an online screen. The three large firms publish their own pages and practice cases, so the backing is strong.

shows.label: A structured answer to a client case
shows.means: Clarify the objective. Break the problem into parts that fit this case, not a stock framework. Think aloud, work the data and commit to an answer.
artifacts: A written issue tree for a published practice case
A recording of yourself answering one of the firms' practice cases

shows.label: Quick sums and market sizing
shows.means: Size a market from a few stated assumptions. Do the arithmetic by hand and say what the number means.
artifacts: A one-page market sizing with every assumption written down
A log of timed mental-maths drills

shows.label: An answer-first recommendation
shows.means: Lead with the answer. Put each supporting point under it. Close a case with a short recommendation.
artifacts: A one-page memo with one governing point
A one-minute recorded recommendation for a practice case

shows.label: Stories from your own experience
shows.means: Pick a few experiences that mattered. Say what your own part was and why you did what you did. Tell them as a conversation, not a script.
artifacts: Short write-ups of several experiences, each with your role and your reasoning

shows.label: A written case you present
shows.means: Take a business challenge. Write up your recommendation over a few days, then present it and take questions.
artifacts: A short written recommendation on one company's problem
A recorded presentation of it

market_research.label: Market Research and Insights Manager
market_research.summary: The one employer source, P&G's consumer insights page, describes the work: purchase data joined with qualitative research to find what drives a business. It does not publish a research work sample, and the only credential found is weak.

shows.label: A study that joins numbers and interviews
shows.means: Pick a product category. Analyze sales or purchase data, talk to real buyers, and name what drives the business. End with what the brand should do.
artifacts: A research report: the question, the design, the data analysis, the interview findings and a recommendation
The analysis file or notebook behind it

shows.label: A read of what an ad or promotion did
shows.means: Take one campaign or price promotion with public or synthetic data. Measure what it changed and say whether it brought new buyers.
artifacts: A short analysis of one campaign or promotion with the method and its limits stated

shows.label: Stories of leading a project
shows.means: Write up times you led a project across teams and solved a problem. Keep each story to the situation, what you did and what changed.
artifacts: Three written behavioral stories from real projects

marketing_manager.label: Marketing Manager
marketing_manager.summary: The sources for marketing managers are the brand ones: a short marketing case, a plan built in a fixed order, and behavioral interviews. Employers describe their process but not a marketing work sample, so the detail comes from student accounts, a course and practitioner writing.

shows.label: A marketing case with a firm recommendation
shows.means: Take a short marketing problem for a real product. Start from the consumer, cover the company, the competitors and the mix, state your assumptions and decide.
artifacts: A one-page written answer to a marketing case
A recorded spoken answer to the same case

shows.label: A marketing plan built in order
shows.means: Pick a real product. Do the research first. Then segment, target and position, set objectives, and only then choose the tactics. Say how the plan reaches more buyers.
artifacts: A marketing plan: research, segments, target, positioning, objectives, tactics
A one-page summary of the plan's main decisions

shows.label: A growth loop for one product
shows.means: Draw how one product grows as a closed loop: each step, and how its output feeds the next round. Model how the loop compounds against a one-off win.
artifacts: A drawn growth loop for a real product
A simple spreadsheet model comparing a loop with a one-off win

shows.label: Stories of leading and getting results
shows.means: Write up times you led people, solved a problem and got a result. Keep each story to the situation, what you did and what changed.
artifacts: Three written behavioral stories from real projects, clubs or jobs

ml_engineer.label: ML / AI Engineer
ml_engineer.summary: ML engineer loops test coding, now often beside an AI assistant, and ML system design. One open fellowship asks for evidence you can ship empirical work. No employer page says what an ML take-home or portfolio project must contain, so the build items lean on books.

shows.label: ML fundamentals
shows.means: Work through knowledge questions on maths, computer science, ML workflows and algorithms. Write your answers out in full.
artifacts: Worked answers to a set of ML knowledge questions

shows.label: An ML system design
shows.means: Design an ML system for one product problem. Cover the training data, the features, how you evaluate, how it deploys, what you monitor and when you retrain. Draw it.
artifacts: A design document for an ML system with a diagram

shows.label: Coding with an AI assistant
shows.means: Solve a coding problem with an AI assistant on screen. Read what it writes, say what is wrong with it and fix it.
artifacts: A solved problem with your notes on what the assistant got wrong and how you corrected it

shows.label: An empirical ML project, written up
shows.means: Ask one question about a model. Run the experiments, report what you found and publish the write-up with the code. Know it well enough to discuss in depth.
artifacts: A public write-up or short paper of an empirical ML experiment
The code and results behind it

shows.label: An application on a foundation model with an evaluation set
shows.means: Build a small application on a foundation model. Write an evaluation set for it and report how it scores before and after your changes.
artifacts: A working application built on a foundation model
An evaluation set with results

operations_manager.label: Operations Manager
operations_manager.summary: One employer program says it screens on leadership judgment and problem solving. The rest comes from candidate reports and a credential's project requirement, so every item is thin.

shows.label: Leadership stories
shows.means: Write up times you led people and owned a result. Tie each one to the employer's stated leadership principles.
artifacts: Several short write-ups, each with your part and the outcome

shows.label: An operations analysis you present
shows.means: Take a dataset and an operations question. Work it in SQL or a spreadsheet, then present what you would do.
artifacts: A short deck from a dataset with a recommendation
The queries or the spreadsheet behind it

shows.label: A finished process improvement project
shows.means: Pick a process you can measure. Define the problem, measure it, find the cause, fix it and show it held.
artifacts: A project report that follows define, measure, analyze, improve, control
A sign-off from the person who owns the process

pe_associate.label: Private Equity Associate
pe_associate.summary: No private equity firm's hiring page was found. A valuation textbook covers the models and one venture firm's published memos show what an investment recommendation looks like.

shows.label: A valuation of a real company
shows.means: Value one public company three ways: comparable companies, precedent transactions and discounted cash flow. Say why the answers differ.
artifacts: A comparable companies table and a precedents table
A discounted cash flow model
A one-page summary of the value range

shows.label: A leveraged buyout model
shows.means: Pick a company a buyer could take private. Model the purchase, the debt and the return at exit.
artifacts: A leveraged buyout model for one company with the returns under a few cases

shows.label: An investment memo
shows.means: Pick a company. Write the recommendation: the business, the market, the diligence you did, the risks and the terms you would propose.
artifacts: A written investment memo on one real company

pm.label: Product Manager
pm.summary: PM loops test product sense, analytical thinking and leadership. The newer programs and startup work trials ask for something shipped.

shows.label: Product sense
shows.means: Pick a user. Name their problem. Choose what to build and say what you cut.
artifacts: A written teardown of a real product
A redesign of one feature with the trade-offs stated

shows.label: Analytical thinking
shows.means: Say why the product exists. Define metrics someone could query. Pick one North Star metric, add guardrails, and set one team goal.
artifacts: A product rationale for a product you use
A metric framework with a North Star metric and guardrails
One team goal with the options you weighed
A trade-off decision with what would change your mind

shows.label: A plan for an open product problem
shows.means: Size the problem. Name who is affected. List solutions, put them in order, and say how you would measure success.
artifacts: A short deck: what you would build, in what order, and why
Ranked experiment ideas for a real product's new-user flow, three worked out

shows.label: Evidence from real users
shows.means: Talk to real users before you propose anything. Tie each idea to what they said.
artifacts: Notes from five user conversations with what changed in your plan

shows.label: Something shipped
shows.means: Build a small product, put it in front of users, and say what you learned from them.
artifacts: A working product with a 60-second demo
Short answers: the problem, what you built, your part, the result, what users taught you

shows.label: Leadership stories
shows.means: Write up your largest projects with context and results. Include a failure, a disagreement you resolved, and research that changed your plan.
artifacts: Three to five project write-ups with numbers

pmm.label: Product Marketing Manager
pmm.summary: PMM loops test positioning and a go-to-market case, often as a take-home deck presented to a panel, plus a small portfolio of written pieces.

shows.label: Positioning
shows.means: Say who the product is for, what they would use instead, what only it does, and why that matters to them.
artifacts: A positioning document for a real product
A sales pitch outline built from it

shows.label: A go-to-market or launch plan
shows.means: Plan a launch for a real product: the audience, the message, the channels, the measures.
artifacts: A launch plan as a deck or document you can present

shows.label: Launch writing
shows.means: Write the piece a launch needs: a blog post, a press release or a one-page data sheet.
artifacts: Two or three published pieces for real or imagined launches

shows.label: A marketing case with a point of view
shows.means: Take a brand or product problem. Structure it, weigh the options and commit to one recommendation.
artifacts: A written answer to a marketing case with a clear recommendation

shows.label: Material a seller can use
shows.means: Turn the positioning into something a salesperson would use on a call.
artifacts: A one-page battle card or pitch outline

product_designer.label: Product / UX Designer
product_designer.summary: Design loops rest on the portfolio: three to five case studies that show process, not only the final screens. Then a live design exercise and a critique of a shipped app.

shows.label: A case study that shows process
shows.means: State the user problem. Show the sketches, the directions you rejected, the final design, your part and the result.
artifacts: One case study in a consistent template; three to five make the portfolio

shows.label: A design exercise, worked end to end
shows.means: From a one-line prompt: the goal, the audience, their needs, ranked ideas, a sketched solution, how you would measure it.
artifacts: A written-up design exercise with sketches of several directions

shows.label: A critique of a shipped app
shows.means: Pick an app you use. Say what works, what does not, and why the team likely chose it.
artifacts: A written or recorded critique of one app

shows.label: One interaction, designed for a real product
shows.means: Design one named interaction in a real product, in its own design language.
artifacts: A prototype of the interaction with the states and edge cases

shows.label: Research that feeds a decision
shows.means: Write the questions, talk to a few users, and say what the findings change.
artifacts: A research plan, an interview guide and a one-page findings summary

product_engineer.label: Product Engineer
product_engineer.summary: Product engineer hiring asks for something built and shipped, then a small version of the job: a paid trial day or a real feature. The detail comes from PostHog's own pages, a practitioner survey of startup work trials and a secondary account of one LinkedIn program; this is startup practice.

shows.label: A product real people used
shows.means: Build a product or feature and ship it. Get real people to use it. Link it where a reader can try it.
artifacts: A live side project with a public link and public code
A 60-second demo video of it

shows.label: A short account of what you built
shows.means: Answer in a few lines each: the problem, what you built, your role, the impact, the stack and how you used AI, and the main thing you learned from users.
artifacts: Six short written answers about one shipped project

shows.label: A small feature in a real codebase
shows.means: Take an open-source or forked codebase. Build one small feature or fix real bugs in a set time. Write down what you put first and why, then take feedback on it.
artifacts: A small shipped feature or bug fix in a real or forked codebase
A short written note on what you chose to do first and what you left out

shows.label: A contribution to the company's product
shows.means: Pick a company with a public repository or docs. Fix something, or file an issue that helps. Do it before you apply.
artifacts: A merged pull request, a docs fix or a useful issue on the target company's product

product_ops.label: Product Operations
product_ops.summary: No employer publishes a product ops loop. One practitioner's hiring article says past process, OKR or data work is the evidence; a vendor glossary and a book site describe the function. The backing is thin throughout.

shows.label: A process you designed
shows.means: Pick one way a product team works that wastes time. Say who is involved and what goes wrong. Design the new process and say how you would get the teams to use it.
artifacts: A one-page process write-up: the problem, the new steps, who does what
A short write-up of a process or OKR cycle you ran for a team or student group

shows.label: Product data turned into a decision
shows.means: Take product usage data and one question a product leader has. Pull the data, analyse it and say what the team should do.
artifacts: A short analysis of a product dataset with the SQL behind it
A one-page recommendation for a product leader

product_owner.label: Product Owner
product_owner.summary: No employer loop or early-career program is on record for product owners. The Scrum Guide defines the work and one certification outline lists the knowledge; neither is a hiring process.

shows.label: A product goal and an ordered backlog
shows.means: Write the goal for a product. Write the backlog items so a team could pick them up. Put them in order and say why the top ones give the most value.
artifacts: A product goal
An ordered product backlog with clearly written items and the reason for the order

shows.label: A vision and a release plan
shows.means: State the product vision. Forecast what ships in which release. Say which stakeholders and customers you would keep informed and how.
artifacts: A one-page product vision with a release forecast

re_acquisitions.label: Real Estate Acquisitions Associate
re_acquisitions.summary: No real estate employer's hiring page was found. A software certification, a modelling site and a student competition all point at the same work: a property cash-flow model and a proposal with financials that hold up.

shows.label: An acquisition model for one property
shows.means: Pick a real property. Build its cash flows in a spreadsheet and say what you would pay.
artifacts: An acquisition pro forma in Excel for one property type

shows.label: A proposal for a real site
shows.means: Take a real site. Say what should be built or bought there, back it with market data and financials, and present it.
artifacts: A narrative and a pro forma for one site
A recorded presentation of the proposal

re_development.label: Real Estate Development Manager
re_development.summary: No developer's hiring page was found. A graduate student competition sets the clearest standard: a development proposal for a real site with financials that hold up, presented to a jury. A modelling site and a software certification cover the pro forma.

shows.label: A development pro forma
shows.means: Pick a site and a building program. Model the costs, the cash flows and the return in a spreadsheet.
artifacts: A development pro forma in Excel with market-based assumptions

shows.label: A development proposal for a real site
shows.means: Take a large real site. Decide what to build, show the design, back it with market-feasible financials and present it. Work with people from another discipline if you can.
artifacts: Boards and a narrative for the proposal
The pro forma behind it
A recorded presentation

security_engineer.label: Security Engineer
security_engineer.summary: No employer publishes a security engineer loop. One Google engineer's study notes, the OWASP Top 10, one penetration-testing credential and the public CTF record describe the work; most items rest on a single one of these.

shows.label: Small security tools
shows.means: Write small tools in Python: a log parser, a port scanner, a cipher. Explain what each one does and where it fails.
artifacts: A repository of small security tools with a README for each

shows.label: A threat model
shows.means: Pick a system. Draw how data flows through it and mark the trust boundaries. List what could go wrong and what you would fix first.
artifacts: A threat model of one system with a data-flow diagram and trust boundaries

shows.label: Web vulnerabilities found, exploited and fixed
shows.means: Take a deliberately vulnerable application or your own. Find the common web risks in it, exploit each one, then fix it and say how.
artifacts: A write-up that finds, exploits and fixes web application issues by risk category
A code review mapped to the same categories

shows.label: A penetration test of a lab network
shows.means: Work through practice lab machines. Enumerate, get initial access, escalate privileges and pivot. Write the report a client would read.
artifacts: Proof of compromise for each lab machine
A written penetration-test report

shows.label: CTF write-ups
shows.means: Enter capture-the-flag events. Publish how you solved each challenge.
artifacts: Published write-ups of solved challenges
A team profile with placements

software_engineer.label: Software Engineer
software_engineer.summary: Big Tech still tests algorithms and system design, now with an AI assistant in the room. Startups hire on real work: a bug fixed in an unfamiliar codebase, an API integrated from its docs, a trial project.

shows.label: Coding fundamentals
shows.means: Solve problems with the core data structures and algorithms. Explain your approach and its cost as you go.
artifacts: A tracked set of solved problems with notes on the pattern each uses

shows.label: Work in a codebase you did not write
shows.means: Find and fix a real bug in an open-source project. Explain how you found it.
artifacts: A merged or open pull request with the reasoning written up

shows.label: Build against an API from its docs
shows.means: Read the documentation of a real API and ship something small that uses it.
artifacts: A working integration with a short README

shows.label: System design
shows.means: State the requirements. Estimate the load. Draw the parts and say what you traded away.
artifacts: A design write-up with a diagram, estimates and trade-offs for a system you built or use

shows.label: Work with an AI assistant and judge its output
shows.means: Build with an AI tool. Review what it wrote, find what is wrong, and say why.
artifacts: A project log showing where you corrected or rejected the assistant's code

shows.label: A shipped project with other people
shows.means: Ship a small feature that real users touch, ideally with at least one other person.
artifacts: A deployed project, its repository, and a note on who did what

shows.label: Stories with results
shows.means: Write up past work with numbers. Include a failure and what you learned.
artifacts: A bank of stories in situation, action, result form

solutions_engineer.label: Solutions Engineer
solutions_engineer.summary: Solutions engineer loops end in a demo to a panel playing the customer, built on discovery. One book sets out the craft; the loop itself comes from candidate reports and prep vendors, and no employer page describes it.

shows.label: A discovery call
shows.means: Before you show anything, find out what the customer's business needs. Plan the questions and run the call with someone playing the buyer.
artifacts: A discovery plan for one real company
A recorded mock discovery call

shows.label: A whiteboard explanation
shows.means: Explain a technical solution on a whiteboard to someone who is not technical. Tell it as a story and take questions as you go.
artifacts: A recorded whiteboard walk-through of one solution

shows.label: A demo fitted to one customer
shows.means: Take a scenario about one customer. Build a demo of a real product around their problem, present it to people playing the customer, and answer their hard questions accurately.
artifacts: A recorded demo of a real product tailored to a written customer scenario
Your answers to the hard questions you expect

shows.label: A qualified opportunity
shows.means: Take one realistic opportunity. Say who decides, on what criteria, by what process, what the pain costs and who is on your side.
artifacts: A deal sheet filled in for one opportunity

strategic_finance.label: Strategic Finance Manager
strategic_finance.summary: No source describes a strategic finance loop. An exam outline names the modelling work and a practitioner newsletter supplies the metrics, benchmarks and planning formats; neither says what an interview asks.

shows.label: A forecast model with sensitivities
shows.means: Build a model for a real software company. Project revenue, state the drivers, and show how the result moves when they change.
artifacts: A spreadsheet model with a revenue projection and a sensitivity table

shows.label: A metrics and benchmark view of one company
shows.means: Pick a public software company. Work out its main metrics and set them against benchmarks.
artifacts: A one-page metrics sheet with benchmarks and what they say about the plan

strategy_manager.label: Strategy Manager
strategy_manager.summary: In-house strategy teams do not publish their loops. A job posting, a vendor guide and candidate reports point to a case on the company's own problem and a take-home analysis that you present.

shows.label: A structured answer to a company's own problem
shows.means: Take a real question a company faces, such as build, buy or partner. Lay out the options, put them in order and commit to one.
artifacts: A written answer to a case about a real company

shows.label: An analysis that ends in a recommendation
shows.means: Define the problem. Run the analysis on real data, build the model and recommend what to do, as you would to an executive.
artifacts: A deck or memo from a dataset with a model behind it
A recorded walk-through of the recommendation

shows.label: Answer-first writing
shows.means: Lead with the answer. Put each supporting point under it.
artifacts: A one-page memo or short deck with one governing point

supply_chain.label: Supply Chain Manager
supply_chain.summary: Employer programs here test leadership judgment and behavioral examples, not supply chain technique. The technique comes from the supply chain credentials' outlines: forecasting, sales and operations planning, inventory, logistics and risk.

shows.label: Stories of leading and owning an outcome
shows.means: Write up times you led people, used judgment under pressure and owned a result. Keep each story to the situation, what you did and what changed.
artifacts: Three written behavioral stories from real projects, clubs or jobs

shows.label: A demand forecast and an inventory plan
shows.means: Take sales history for a few products. Forecast demand, set inventory levels, and write the supply plan a monthly planning meeting would agree.
artifacts: A spreadsheet with the forecast, its error and the inventory levels
A one-page plan matching supply to demand

shows.label: A supply chain mapped with its risks
shows.means: Map one product's chain from suppliers to customer. Mark where it can break and say what you would do about each risk.
artifacts: A supply chain map for one product with a short list of risks and responses

shows.label: An emissions inventory for a supply chain
shows.means: Set the boundary for one organization. Gather activity data, apply emission factors and total the emissions by scope, including the value chain.
artifacts: A greenhouse gas inventory: boundaries, activity data, emission factors, totals by scope

sustainability.label: Sustainability and ESG Manager
sustainability.summary: No employer program or loop was found for sustainability. The standard-setters' own pages say what the work is: a greenhouse gas inventory, a materiality assessment and a link from sustainability issues to the financial statements.

shows.label: A greenhouse gas inventory
shows.means: Pick an organization. Set the boundary, gather activity data, apply emission factors and total the emissions for scopes 1, 2 and 3.
artifacts: An inventory workbook: boundaries, activity data, emission factors, totals by scope
A short note on the method and the gaps in the data

shows.label: A materiality assessment
shows.means: Pick a public company. Decide which sustainability topics matter most to it and its investors, and map each to the reporting standard that covers it.
artifacts: A materiality assessment for one company
A content index mapping its disclosures to a reporting standard

shows.label: A sustainability issue traced to the financials
shows.means: Take one company. Find the sustainability risks and opportunities that move its financial performance, and show where each lands in the statements and the valuation.
artifacts: A case memo linking two or three sustainability issues to revenue, cost or asset values

tpm.label: Technical Program Manager
tpm.summary: TPM loops test system design, program sense and stories from past programs told with numbers. Amazon publishes its loop in detail; Meta's and Google's round names come from third-party summaries. Nothing is handed in except Amazon's written piece.

shows.label: A system design
shows.means: Design a software system for a stated need. Ask what it must do first. Say how it stays reliable and how it scales, and name the trade-offs.
artifacts: A design write-up with a diagram for one system
The questions you asked and the trade-offs you chose

shows.label: A program plan
shows.means: Plan a program that spans several teams. List the milestones, the dependencies and the technical risks. Say who hears what, how often, and when you escalate.
artifacts: A program plan: milestones, dependencies, risks, an escalation path
A one-page status report for it

shows.label: A technical project you can defend in depth
shows.means: Run a technical project with other people from start to finish. Write up what was built, how it works, what went wrong and the result in numbers. Be ready for an engineer to dig into any part.
artifacts: A written retrospective of one technical project with quantified results
A walk-through of its design that holds up to follow-up questions

shows.label: Stories with numbers
shows.means: Write up a few past wins and difficulties. Give the situation, what you did, the result in numbers and what you learned. Include one about a conflict and one about moving people you did not manage.
artifacts: Three to five project stories with quantified results and learnings

transformation.label: Transformation Manager
transformation.summary: No employer publishes a transformation loop. One consulting firm's interview page lists this role, and three credentials describe the work: a change plan, an improvement project and a record of projects led.

shows.label: A structured answer to a client case
shows.means: Take a typical client problem. Build an approach that fits this case, not a stock framework, and commit to an answer.
artifacts: A recording of yourself answering a published practice case

shows.label: A change plan for a real project
shows.means: Pick a change under way in an organization you know. Assess the risk and how ready people are, then plan sponsors, stakeholders and communication.
artifacts: A risk and readiness assessment for one change
A change management strategy with its core plans

shows.label: A finished process improvement project
shows.means: Pick a process you can measure. Define the problem, measure it, find the cause, fix it and show it held.
artifacts: A project report that follows define, measure, analyze, improve, control
A sign-off from the person who owns the process

shows.label: A record of projects you led
shows.means: For each project, say what you were responsible for: the plan, the decisions, the delivery and the outcome. Be ready to talk through your own part in detail.
artifacts: A write-up per project with your responsibility and the result

ux_researcher.label: UX Researcher
ux_researcher.summary: UX research loops ask you to design a study on the spot and to present a past study, ending on what it changed. Google's own article and Nielsen Norman Group's portfolio guide are first-hand; Meta's loop comes from a prep vendor.

shows.label: A study design
shows.means: Take a product question. State the research questions, choose the method and the people to recruit, and say what each choice trades off.
artifacts: A research plan with questions, method and sampling
A screener and an interview or usability-test guide

shows.label: A survey, designed and analysed
shows.means: Write a survey for one research question. Field it, analyse the answers and say what they do and do not show.
artifacts: A survey instrument with the analysis of its results

shows.label: A study run from plan to findings
shows.means: Run a real study on a product. Plan it, talk to users or test with them, synthesise what you saw and report a few key findings in plain language.
artifacts: A study plan and the test tasks or interview guide
An affinity diagram or other synthesis
A short findings report that feeds one decision

shows.label: A case study presentation
shows.means: Present one study to a panel inside a time limit. Tell it as a story, show your decisions and end on what changed because of the research. Cut it and rehearse it.
artifacts: A timed deck on one study that ends on its impact
A recording of yourself giving it

shows.label: A research portfolio
shows.means: Choose three to five projects that show a range of methods. For each, give the context, your role, the key findings and the impact. Credit your teammates.
artifacts: A portfolio of three to five studies with their artifacts: plans, reports, personas, journey maps
An impact line for each: a metric or a before-and-after

vc_associate.label: Venture Capital Associate
vc_associate.summary: No venture firm's hiring page was found. One firm publishes its investment memos and one book covers how deals are put together, so both items are thin.

shows.label: An investment memo
shows.means: Pick a startup. Write the recommendation to a partnership: the company, the market, the diligence you did, the risks and the terms you would propose.
artifacts: A written investment memo on one real startup

shows.label: How a venture deal is put together
shows.means: Take one financing. Set out its structure and say what each main term does for the founder and the investor.
artifacts: A one-page plain-words summary of one deal's structure
